data.title: Vail Resorts' biggest investor backs company in fight with activist Oasis
data.description:
By Svea Herbst-Bayliss

Vail Resorts won support on Friday from its largest investor as it faces increasing pressure from activist Oasis Management to make operational changes including the possible sale of some mountain assets.

Ron Baron said in a statement his firm Baron Capital, which owned 18% of Vail's stock at the end of June, will back Vail's management at next month's boardroom election and will vote for Vail Resorts' nominees.

Baron added that he believes Vail CEO Rob Katz "has the right strategy to return to sustainable earnings growth."

BOARDROOM FIGHT

Vail, which owns mountain resorts and ski areas in Utah, Colorado and the northeastern United States, is facing off against Oasis, an activist investor and Vail's fourth-biggest shareholder with a 9% stake at the end of September, in one of the year's most contentious boardroom fights.

Oasis wants changes, including the possible sale of some mountain assets, and in September nominated four director candidates, including former Olympic ski champion Picabo Street and former Walt Disney CEO Bob Chapek.

Vail, which has a market value of $5 billion, is urging investors to vote for its nine directors and argues its multi-year transformation strategy, dubbed "Epic Experience", will pay off. It has already made changes like upgrading its quick service menu items, improving ticket purchasing and offering advance purchase discounts. It has also upgraded its ski school and lessons.

'SHORT-SIGHTED' EFFORT

Since January, Vail's stock price has climbed 13% and is trading at $151.37 on Friday. But over the last five years, the stock tumbled nearly 50% and the company said last month that full fiscal-year profit nearly halved compared with a year earlier. Record low snowfall brought fewer guests to Vail's mountains and has weighed on earnings.

Baron also referenced a simmering fight around billionaire tech company Cloudflare Chief Executive Matthew Prince, who has been pushing to buy Park City Mountain Resort from Vail.

"I also have serious concerns about Oasis' coordination with Matthew Prince," Baron wrote, adding he views Prince's effort to have Vail sell him Park City as "short-sighted and destructive to long-term shareholder value."

A representative for Oasis said: "It's not surprising that the board would try to distract shareholders from their poor performance by making misleading statements — from false accusations about coordination to asserting that the board has done a great job. We continue to believe in the value of the assets and the need for board refreshment."

Prince could not be reached for comment.

(17:48 GMT) Nasdaq Newcomer Sees Growth for Oil Well Logging Technology — Interview

By Anthony Harrup

Oil well logging technology company GOWell Energy Technology sees increasing demand for its equipment and expects its recent listing on Nasdaq to help in its bid to grow, according to the company's chief executive.

GOWell Energy Technology began trading on Nasdaq at the end of September following a business combination with Inflection Point Acquisition Corp. V, a special purpose acquisition company.

The company designs and manufactures equipment to monitor for leaks, corrosion, or other defects in wells. It doesn't provide field services, but oil-field services companies deploy its technology, CEO Guillaume Borrel said in an interview.

GOWell's latest technology stays within the tubing of a well and can see behind the outer casing without the need to remove the tubing, Borrel said. "That's massive savings and these are our innovations."

GOWell, with headquarters in Singapore and a principal office in Houston where it carries out its research and development, expects to see solid sales growth amid strong demand for well logging.

Its main operating subsidiary reported revenue of $33.8 million, a 43% increase over the first half of 2025, and for the full year expects revenue between $60 million and $68 million, up from $47.2 million in 2025.

Advantages of GOWell's decision to go public include greater visibility in the global marketplace and easier access to capital markets if needed for organic growth or to pursue acquisitions, Borrel said. "We do have an ambitious M&A program and plan."

Among the reasons for the optimism is the demand for well logging technology, particularly at a time when energy security is becoming of major importance, he said. That is driving focus on getting more out of existing infrastructure.

"The wells we have already in the ground, can we open them a bit more, can we squeeze a few more drops out? Can we go back into them and start them up again if they've been shut in?" Borrel said.

That requires well integrity.

"We need to make sure the hydrocarbon stays where it needs to be inside the tubing, and doesn't leak outside, or stuff on the outside doesn't leak inside," Borrel said. "Any operator tries to protect not just the environment but also the actual hydrocarbon they're producing."

Another source of demand for the technology is the decommissioning of wells that need to be properly plugged when they reach the end of their life cycle, he added.

CHAIRMAN'S STATEMENT

For the year ended 30 June 2026

Fairview owns and operates two international schools in Malaysia, in Kuala Lumpur and Johor Bahru. Our priorities are to maintain the quality of education, recruit and retain students, and make effective use of the capacity available at both schools.

Financial Performance

Consolidated revenue increased by 12.2% to £5.99 million (2025: £5.34 million). Growth reflected higher average fees across the two schools, while continued management of operating and administrative costs supported improved operating margins.

Profit before tax and exceptional items rose by approximately 35% to £2.95 million (2025: £2.18 million). Reported profit before tax increased to £2.95 million (2025: £1.30 million), while profit after tax rose to £2.07 million (2025: £0.75 million). The prior year ended 30 June 2025 included £0.88 million of exceptional costs associated with the IPO and pre-IPO group reconstruction. No equivalent exceptional costs were incurred in the year ended 30 June 2026. This accounts for part of the increase in reported profit before tax, alongside the improvement in underlying performance. The Board have not proposed a dividend in respect of the year ended 30 June 2026 but will consider future dividend policy in the light of competing expansion considerations.

Student Enrolment And Capacity

Total student enrolment was 737 in the year ended 30 June 2026, compared with 694 in the previous financial year, an increase of approximately 6%. New enrolments for the academic year ending 30 June 2027 are in line with expectations. We have increased investment in marketing and recruitment and expect these efforts to support further enrolments during the year.

Of currently enrolled students, 37% are in the Primary Years Programme, 53% in the Middle Years Programme and 10% in the Diploma Programme. This gives us opportunities to support students through successive stages of their education and makes retention an important part of our growth strategy.

The capacities of the Kuala Lumpur and Johor Bahru schools are 1,500 and 750 students respectively. Both schools therefore have substantial capacity for growth. Additional enrolments can be accommodated without new capital expenditure, providing scope to improve margins as student numbers increase.

Academic Performance

Academic results remain central to Fairview's appeal to families. For the seventh consecutive year, Fairview Kuala Lumpur was ranked among the top 100 IB schools globally. In the provisional 2026 IB-Schools.com league table, it was ranked joint 38th worldwide and joint 13th in Asia, and was the highest-ranked school in Malaysia for the fourth time. Its students achieved an average IB Diploma Programme score of 38 points.

We continue to support students through bursaries, scholarships and academic awards. Our focus is on combining strong academic standards with accessible education and long-term relationships with the families we serve. Teacher development, student wellbeing and the quality of the learning experience remain priorities.

Education strategy and innovation

The Education Committee supports the Board in shaping Fairview's educational strategy and assessing how new approaches can improve teaching and learning. Its work includes teacher development, curriculum innovation and the responsible use of technology.

A controlled pilot of LIAM, an AI-enabled learning companion, is being used to evaluate its educational effectiveness. The pilot involves approximately 300 Middle Years Programme students in Mathematics and Science across the five Malaysian campuses, together with a matched control group. LIAM uses a question-led approach intended to strengthen critical thinking and student independence, while giving teachers insights into student progress.

Fairview school and wider network

The five Malaysian schools operating under the Fairview brand share educational resources and expertise. Two are owned by the Company; the other three are under common control but outside the Group.

Fairview Kuala Lumpur occupies a 3.5-acre site in Wangsa Maju and offers the Primary Years, Middle Years and Diploma Programmes. It is also the network's headquarters and commercial centre. Fairview Johor Bahru, founded in 2007, occupies a 5-acre campus near the Singapore border and offers the Primary Years and Middle Years Programmes.

The network's educational approach combines the IB curriculum with the ToolBox Skills Programme, the Falcons Leadership Programme, character education and experiential learning. The BeED learning management system supports shared teaching resources, planning and assessment across campuses. Resource sharing helps the schools maintain consistent educational standards and manage costs.

A school in Scotland that operated outside the Group and within the wider Fairview network suspended operations in June 2026 because of adverse trading conditions.

Growth opportunities and outlook

Our immediate priority is organic growth at the existing schools. We aim to build on academic performance, improve recruitment and retention, and maintain careful cost management.

The development of the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone may support demand for international schooling as economic activity and the local population grow. Fairview Johor's location near Singapore provides a basis from which to access that opportunity. Furthermore, looking forward, the Group are considering the possibility of entering into a property development project on its Johor Bharu property, which has land surplus to its immediate educational needs. Specific proposals have not been sought and at this stage the board is discussing the opportunities as part of the Group's overall growth strategy.

We continue to assess selected acquisition and new-school opportunities in Asia and the United Kingdom. Any opportunity must meet our criteria for educational quality, demand and financial sustainability. We will remain selective as we evaluate the potential to apply Fairview's educational model and shared resources to additional schools.

I thank our teachers, staff and leadership teams for their work during the year, and our students, families and shareholders for their continued support.

Notice of the Company's AGM, to be held in December 2026, will be sent to shareholders shortly.

The Company was incorporated on 28 February 2024 and, on 1 July 2024, acquired two companies, Fairview Schools Berhad and Fairview International School Nusajaya Sdn Bhd which own and operate two private independent schools in Malaysia that offer the international baccalaureate programme. Fairview Schools Berhad is located in Kuala Lumpur, the capital of Malaysia, and Fairview International School Nusajaya Sdn Bhd is located in the southern state of Johor close to the border with Singapore. These schools trade under the Fairview brand which was created in 1978. The school in Kuala Lumpur is the largest school that uses the Fairview brand, whilst the school in Johor was acquired as it focuses on the expatriate market in Singapore and so is more internationally focused than the remaining schools which are more focused on the domestic Malaysian market.

The Directors have also considered reasonably possible downside scenarios, including lower student enrolments and associated fee income, increased operating costs and higher financing costs. Under both the base case and the reasonably possible downside scenarios, the Group is forecast to maintain sufficient liquidity throughout the assessment period, with a minimum forecast cash balance of £1.2 million under the base case and £150,000 under the downside scenario.

The Directors have identified a number of actions available to manage liquidity should trading performance fall below forecast. These include reducing discretionary expenditure, deferring non-essential capital expenditure, managing the timing of working capital expenditure and utilising leasing or hire-purchase arrangements for capital equipment where appropriate.

Having considered the Group's financial position, current and expected trading, cash flow forecasts, available financing facilities, debt servicing requirements, covenant headroom, reasonably possible downside scenarios and the mitigating actions available to management, the Directors have a reasonable expectation that the Group and the Company have adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future and for a period of at least twelve months from the date of approval of these financial statements.

Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) Statement

As a public company operating schools and education facilities, the Company acknowledges its obligations under the Financial Conduct Authority's Listing Rule 6.6.6R regarding climate-related disclosures consistent with the recommendations of the Task Force on Climate-Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). This statement provides a summary of the Group's current position with reference to the four TCFD pillars: Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics and Targets. As a business operating in a highly regulated and evolving sector,  our approach reflects the nature of our business, including the operation and maintenance of school buildings, transportation, energy use, supply chains, student and staff safety, and business continuity. Fairview's focus has been on building a stable and compliant operating model. It does, however, recognise the increasing importance of environmental factors and are committed to progressively enhancing its climate-related governance and disclosure practices over time.

Governance

The Board of Directors is responsible for overseeing climate-related risks and opportunities. Given the Company's size and the direct involvement of Board members in day-to-day operations, climate-related issues are monitored alongside other operational and regulatory matters. To date, climate-related risks have not formed a material part of the Board's formal consideration of strategy, budgets, performance objectives or capital expenditure. This is primarily due to the nature of the Company business.

Nonetheless, the Board remains mindful of the importance of aligning with climate goals. It has acknowledged that, as the business develops, more structured oversight mechanisms must be developed. These will include clear internal objectives, regular reviews, and progress tracking against climate-related performance indicators.

Strategy

The Group recognises that climate-related risks and opportunities will play a more prominent role in its future strategic and operational planning. The immediate impact of climate change on our operations is currently limited, we consider climate-related risks across our short-, medium-, and long-term planning horizons.

Relevant physical risks may include:

·    Extreme heat affecting students, staff, and school facilities;

·    Flooding, storms, wildfires, and other severe weather events;

·    Water scarcity or disruption;

·    Damage to buildings, equipment, and infrastructure; and

·    Disruption to transportation, utilities, and school operations.

Relevant transition risks may include:

·    Changes in climate-related laws and regulations;

·    Increasing energy and operating costs;

·    Requirements relating to building efficiency and emissions;

·    Changes in stakeholder expectations; and

·    Availability and cost of low-carbon technologies and services.

Climate-related opportunities may include improving energy efficiency, installing renewable energy systems, reducing operating costs, enhancing building resilience, improving indoor environmental quality, and strengthening continuity of educational services.

We seek to incorporate these considerations into capital planning, facilities management, procurement, emergency preparedness, insurance, and business continuity planning. Where appropriate, climate-related risks and opportunities are considered in connection with acquisitions, new construction, renovations, and long-term asset management.

In the future, the Board expects to give greater weight to climate-related considerations when reviewing strategic decisions, including materials sourcing, logistics, and supplier partnerships. For example, rising consumer and regulatory expectations around recyclability and carbon footprint may shape our strategy, while increased scrutiny on supplier emissions could influence our procurement policies. As the business matures, climate performance may become integrated into strategic KPIs, investment decisions, and brand positioning, as this will support long-term competitiveness in an environmentally conscious marketplace.

Risk Management

The Company does not yet maintain a standalone climate risk register, and climate-related risks are currently assessed by the Board alongside broader business risks. All principal risk matters are addressed collectively by the Board due to the Company's size and the integrated nature of its management structure. As our governance framework evolves, Fairview intends to formalise climate risk assessment processes in line with broader enterprise risk management practices.

Identified risks are assessed based on their potential effect on:

·    School operations and educational services;

·    The health and safety of students and employees;

·    Financial performance and capital requirements;

·    Property and equipment;

·    Compliance obligations;

·    Reputation and stakeholder confidence; and

·    Business continuity

Where material risks are identified, management develops mitigation or adaptation measures, assigns accountability, and monitors progress. These measures may include facility upgrades, emergency response procedures, energy-management programs, supplier engagement, insurance coverage, and diversification of critical services.

As part of its broader risk management efforts, the Company intends to introduce more structured processes to identify, evaluate, and mitigate climate-related risks. This includes building internal capacity, formalising risk governance procedures, and integrating these into enterprise risk management as part of the Group's evolution.

Metrics and Targets

The Company has not yet developed climate-specific metrics or targets. Several practical factors have contributed to this:

●     Supply chain volatility has complicated data collection and environmental performance tracking;

●     Resource constraints have required prioritisation of commercial, regulatory and financial status over environmental concerns;

●     Climate-related matters have not been integrated into business KPIs, capital allocation decisions or performance reviews.

However, the Company is beginning to monitor climate-related metrics appropriate to its operations, including:

·    Energy consumption;

·    Greenhouse gas emissions;

·    Energy intensity of facilities;

·    Water consumption;

·    Waste generation and diversion;

·    Exposure of facilities to climate-related hazards; and

·    Operational disruptions caused by severe weather.

Revenue recognition is presumed to be a fraud risk under ISA (UK) 240. For the Group, revenue principally comprises school fees and other income generated from its education operations.

Given the volume of student billings and the timing of fee recognition across academic terms, there is a risk that revenue may be recognised in the incorrect accounting period or recorded prematurely or fictitiously, resulting in an overstatement of revenue and profit. Particular focus was therefore placed on the occurrence, accuracy and cut-off of revenue, including the appropriate treatment of deposits and fees received in advance.

Our procedures included the following:

●     Substantive Testing of Revenue and Cut-off:

We performed substantive audit procedures over revenue recognised during the year, including cut-off testing to assess whether revenue transactions were accurately recorded in the appropriate accounting period. Based on the procedures performed, we identified no material misstatements or evidence of revenue transactions being omitted, incorrectly recognised or recorded in the wrong reporting period. Substantive testing of school fee revenue and other operating income, including enrolment/billing support, cut-off testing, journal entry testing and review of related deposits and unearned fees.

●     Assessment of Revenue Recognition Policies:

We evaluated management's revenue recognition policies, specifically those relating to student fees and associated income streams, to assess their compliance with the applicable financial reporting framework and whether they had been consistently applied.

Our procedures also included reviewing and evaluating the work performed by the component auditor on revenue recognition, including the audit approach adopted, procedures undertaken and conclusions reached.

Based on our assessment and the audit evidence obtained, we concluded that the revenue recognition policies had been appropriately applied and that no material misstatements were identified in the revenue recognised in the financial statements.

●     Review of Material Manual Journals Posted to Revenue:

We examined material manual journal entries posted to revenue to assess their validity, underlying business rationale and appropriateness of recognition. Based on the procedures performed, we identified no evidence of inappropriate revenue recognition or material misstatements arising from the journal entries reviewed.

Our procedures also did not identify any evidence of unrecorded revenue-generating transactions or agreements that would require adjustment to revenue recognised in the financial statements.

Based on the audit procedures performed and the evidence obtained, we concluded that the identified risks of material misstatement due to fraud in revenue recognition had been appropriately addressed and reduced to an acceptably low level, providing sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support our conclusions in accordance with ISA 240.

We identified management override of controls as a presumed significant risk of material misstatement due to fraud under ISA 240, recognising management's ability to override established controls, manipulate financial reporting and potentially misappropriate assets.

In addition to the procedures outlined in the Auditor's Responsibilities for the Audit of the Financial Statements section of our audit report, we performed enhanced audit procedures specifically designed to address this risk.

These included:

●   Significant accounting judgements and estimates: Applied heightened professional scepticism to areas involving significant management judgement and estimation, assessing the reasonableness of underlying assumptions and considering indicators of potential management bias.

Going concern

The financial statements have been prepared on a going concern basis, which assumes that the Group and the Company will continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future.

For the year ended 30 June 2026, the Group generated profit before taxation of £2.952 million (2025: £1.300 million) and operating profit of £3.670 million (2025: £2.957 million). At 30 June 2026, the Group had cash and cash equivalents of £0.151 million (2025: £0.163 million), current assets of £7.649 million and current liabilities of £10.153 million, resulting in net current liabilities of £2.504 million. Total bank borrowings at the reporting date were £10.597 million.

The Directors have prepared cash flow forecasts covering the period to 31 December 2027, which extends for at least twelve months from the expected date of approval of these financial statements. In assessing going concern, the Directors have considered expected student enrolments and fee income, operating expenditure, payroll costs, capital expenditure, debt servicing obligations and the availability of existing and post-year-end financing facilities.

Subsequent to the year end, subsidiaries of the Group secured new financing facilities from Alliance Bank Malaysia comprising RM70 million of Murabahah facilities and RM22.7 million of conventional financing facilities, equivalent in aggregate to approximately £17.2 million. The facilities are secured by first legal charges over properties of the relevant subsidiaries, bear interest based on BFR/ECOF plus margins ranging from 1.5% to 2.25% per annum and are repayable by monthly instalments following full drawdown. The facilities provide additional funding for the working capital requirements of the subsidiaries. In addition, in assessing the Group's working-capital requirements, the Directors have also considered the timing of school fee collections and the level and expected settlement of school fee deposits and fees received in advance.

The Directors have also considered reasonably possible downside scenarios, including lower student enrolments and associated fee income, increased operating costs and higher financing costs. Under both the base case and the reasonably possible downside scenarios, the Group is forecast to maintain sufficient liquidity throughout the assessment period, with a minimum forecast cash balance of £1.2 million under the base case and £150,000 under the downside scenario.

The Group was in compliance with the relevant financial covenants at the date of this assessment and is forecast to remain compliant throughout the going concern assessment period, with appropriate headroom under both the base case and reasonably possible downside scenarios.

The Directors have identified a number of actions available to manage liquidity should trading performance fall below forecast. These include reducing discretionary expenditure, deferring non-essential capital expenditure, managing the timing of working capital expenditure and utilising leasing or hire-purchase arrangements for capital equipment where appropriate.

Having considered the Group's financial position, current and expected trading, cash flow forecasts, available financing facilities, debt servicing requirements, covenant headroom, reasonably possible downside scenarios and the mitigating actions available to management, the Directors have a reasonable expectation that the Group and the Company have adequate resources to continue in operational existence for the foreseeable future and for a period of at least twelve months from the date of approval of these financial statements.

The Directors have therefore continued to adopt the going concern basis of accounting in preparing these financial statements.

2.5 Impairment of Non-Financial Assets

The Group assesses at each reporting date whether there is an indication that an asset may be impaired. If any such indication exists, or when an annual impairment assessment for an asset is required, the Group makes an estimate of the asset's recoverable amount.

An asset's recoverable amount is the higher of its fair value, less costs to sell and its value in use. For the purpose of assessing impairment, assets are grouped at the lowest levels for which there are separately identifiable cash-generating units ("CGU").

In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash flows expected to be generated by the asset are discounted to their present value using a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to the asset. Where the carrying amount of an asset exceeds its recoverable amount, the asset is written down to its recoverable amount. Impairment losses recognised in respect of a CGU or groups of CGUs are allocated first to reduce the carrying amount of any goodwill allocated to those units or groups of units and then, to reduce the carrying amount of the other assets in the unit or groups of units on a pro-rata basis.

Impairment losses are recognised in profit or loss.

An assessment is made at each reporting date as to whether there is any indication that previously recognised impairment losses may no longer exist or may have decreased. A previously recognised impairment loss is reversed only if there has been a change in the estimates used to determine the asset's recoverable amount since the last impairment loss was recognised. If that is the case, the carrying amount of the asset is increased to its recoverable amount. That increase cannot exceed the carrying amount that would have been determined, net of depreciation, had no impairment loss been recognised previously. Such reversal is recognised in profit or loss.

2.6 Functional and Foreign Currency

Functional and presentation currency

The individual financial statements of each entity in the Group are measured using the British pound sterling (GBP) currency, which is the presentation currency.

Foreign currency transactions

Transactions in foreign currencies are measured in the respective functional currencies of the Group and are recorded on initial recognition in the functional currencies at exchange rates approximating those prevailing at the transaction dates. Monetary assets and liabilities denominated in foreign currencies are translated at the rate of exchange prevailing at the reporting date. Non-monetary items denominated in foreign currencies that are measured at historical cost are translated using the exchange rates as at the dates of the initial transactions. Non-monetary items denominated in foreign currencies measured at fair value are translated using the exchange rates at the date when the fair value was determined.

2.7 Financial Instruments

Financial assets and financial liabilities are recognised in the statements of financial position when the Group has become a party to the contractual provisions of the instruments.

Financial instruments are classified as financial assets, financial liabilities or equity instruments in accordance with the substance of the contractual arrangement and their definitions in IAS32. Interest, dividends, gains and losses relating to a financial instrument classified as a liability are reported as an expense or income. Distributions to holders of financial instruments classified as equity are charged directly to equity.

A financial instrument is recognised initially at its fair value (other than trade receivables without significant financing component which are measured at transaction price as defined in IFRS 15- Revenue from Contracts with Customers at inception). Transaction costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition or issue of the financial instrument (other than a financial instrument at fair value through profit or loss) are added to/deducted from the fair value on initial recognition, as appropriate. Transaction costs on the financial instrument at fair value through profit or loss are recognised immediately in profit or loss.

Financial instruments recognised in the statements of financial position are disclosed in the individual policy statement associated with each item.

Financial assets

All recognised financial assets are measured subsequently in their entirety at either amortised cost or fair value (through profit or loss, or other comprehensive income), depending on the classification of the financial assets.

The Group determines the classification of their financial assets at initial recognition, and designate all the financial assets as amortised cost. The Group do not have any financial assets carried at fair value (through profit or loss, or other comprehensive income).

Amortised cost (debt instruments)

The financial asset is held for collection of contractual cash flows where those cash flows represent solely payments of principal and interest. Interest income is recognised by applying the effective interest rate to the gross carrying amount of the financial asset. When the asset has subsequently become credit-impaired, the interest income is recognised by applying the effective interest rate to the amortised cost of the financial asset.

The effective interest method is a method of calculating the amortised cost of a financial asset and of allocating interest income over the relevant period. The effective interest rate is the rate that discounts estimated future cash receipts (including all fees and points paid or received that for GBP an integral part of the effective interest rate, transaction costs and other premiums or discounts), excluding expected credit losses, through the expected life of the financial asset or a shorter period (where appropriate).

Financial liabilities

Other financial liabilities are subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method. The effective interest method is a method of calculating the amortised cost of a financial liability and of allocating interest expense over the relevant period. The effective interest rate is the rate that exactly discounts estimated future cash payments (including all fees and points paid or received that form an integral part of the effective interest rate, transaction costs and other premiums or discounts), through the expected life of the financial liability or a shorter period (where appropriate).

Derecognition

A financial asset or part of it is derecognised when, and only when, the contractual rights to the cash flows from the financial asset expire or when it transfers the financial asset and substantially all the risks and rewards of ownership of the asset to another entity.

On derecognition of a financial asset measured at amortised cost, the difference between the carrying amount of the asset and the sum of the consideration received and receivable is recognised in profit or loss.

A financial liability or a part of it is derecognised when, and only when, the obligation specified in the contract is discharged or cancelled or expires. On derecognition of a financial liability, the difference between the carrying amount of the financial liability extinguished or transferred to another party and the consideration paid, including any non-cash assets transferred or liabilities assumed, is recognised in profit or loss.

Offsetting of financial instruments

Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and the net amount is reported in the statement of financial position if there is a currently enforceable legal right to offset the recognised amounts and there is an intention to settle on a net basis, to realise the assets and settle the liabilities simultaneously.

2.8 Expected Credit Losses

The Group recognises a loss allowance for expected credit losses on financial assets that are measured at amortised cost.

The expected credit loss is estimated as the difference between all contractual cash flows that are due to the Group in accordance with the contract and all the cash flows that the Group expect to receive, discounted at the original effective interest rate.

The amount of expected credit losses is updated at each reporting date to reflect changes in credit risk since initial recognition of the respective financial instrument. The Group always recognises lifetime expected credit losses for trade receivables using the simplified approach. The expected credit losses on these financial assets are estimated using a provision matrix based on the Group's historical credit loss experience and are adjusted for forward-looking information (including time value of money where appropriate).

For all other financial instruments, the Group recognises lifetime expected credit losses when there has been a significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition. However, if the credit risk on the financial instrument has not increased significantly since initial recognition, the Group measures the loss allowance for that financial instrument at an amount equal to 12 month expected credit losses.

The Group recognises an impairment gain or loss in profit or loss for all financial instruments with a corresponding adjustment to their carrying amount through a loss allowance account.

2.9 Cash and Cash Equivalents

Cash and cash equivalents comprise cash at bank and on hand and short-term deposits with a maturity of three months or less, which are subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value, net of outstanding bank overdrafts and fixed deposits pledged. For the purpose of the statement of cash flows, cash and cash equivalents are presented net of bank overdrafts and fixed deposits pledged.

2.10 Equity Instruments

Ordinary shares are classified as equity. Dividends on ordinary shares are recognised in equity in the period in which they are approved for payment. The transaction costs of an equity transaction are accounted for as a deduction from equity. Equity transaction costs comprise only those incremental external costs directly attributable to the equity transaction which would otherwise have been avoided.

2.11 Inventories

Inventories are stated at the lower of cost and net realisable value. Cost comprises direct materials, direct labour costs and overheads, where applicable, that have been incurred in bringing the inventories to their present location and condition. Cost is calculated using the weighted average method. Net realisable value represents the estimated selling price less all estimated costs of completion and costs to be incurred in marketing, selling and distribution.

2.12 Leases

The Group assesses whether a contract is or contains a lease, at inception of the contract.

The Group recognises a right-of-use asset and corresponding lease liability with respect to all lease arrangements in which it is the lessee, except for low-value assets and short-term leases with 12 months or less. For these leases, the Group recognises the lease payments as an operating expense on a straight-line method over the term of the lease unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern in which economic benefits from the leased assets are consumed.

The Group recognises a right-of-use asset and a lease liability at the lease commencement date. The right-of-use assets and the associated lease liabilities are presented as a separate line item in the statement of financial position.

The right-of-use asset is initially measured at cost. Cost includes the initial amount of the corresponding lease liability adjusted for any lease payments made at or before the commencement date, plus any initial direct costs incurred less any incentives received.

The right-of-use asset is subsequently measured at cost less accumulated depreciation and any impairment losses and adjusted for any remeasurement of the lease liability.

The depreciation starts from the commencement date of the lease. If the lease transfers ownership of the underlying asset to the Group or the cost of the right-of-use asset reflects that the Group expects to exercise a purchase option, the related right-of-use asset is depreciated over the useful life of the underlying asset. Otherwise, the Group depreciates the right-of-use asset to the earlier of the end of the useful life of the right-of-use asset or the end of the lease term. The estimated useful lives of the right-of-use assets are determined on the same basis as those property, plant and equipment.

The lease liability is initially measured at the present value of the lease payments that are not paid at the commencement date, discounted by using the rate implicit in the lease. If this rate cannot be readily determined, the Group uses its incremental borrowing rate. The lease liability is subsequently measured at amortised cost using the effective interest method. It is remeasured when there is a change in the future lease payments (other than lease modification that is not accounted for as a separate lease) with the corresponding adjustment is made to the carrying amount of the right-of-use asset, or is recognised in profit or loss if the carrying amount has been reduced to zero.

2.13 Revenue and Other Income

Revenue from contracts with customers is recognised by reference to each distinct performance obligation in the contract with customer. Revenue from contracts with customers is measured at its transaction price, being the amount of consideration which the Group expects to be entitled in exchange for transferring promised goods or services to a customer, net of sales and service tax, rebates and discounts.

The Group recognises revenue when (or as) it transfers control over a product or service to customer. An asset is transferred when (or as) the customer obtains control of that asset.

Depending on the substance of the contract, revenue is recognised when the performance obligation is satisfied, which may be at a point in time or over time. The Group transfers control of a good or service at a point in time unless one of the following over time criteria is met:

- The customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits provided as the Group   performs.

- The Group's performance creates or enhances an asset that the customer controls as the asset is created or enhanced.

- The Group's performance does not create an asset with an alternative use and the Group has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date.

Revenue from educational fees

Revenue from educational fee is recognised on a straight-line basis over the duration of the course.

Interest income

Interest income is recognised on an accrual basis using the effective interest method.

Government grants

Grants that compensate the Group for expense incurred are recognised in profit or loss as other income on a systematic basis in the same period in which the expenses are recognised.

Defined Contribution Plan

2.16 Income Tax

Current tax

Current tax assets and liabilities are measured at the amount expected to be recovered from or paid to the taxation authorities. The tax rates and tax laws used to compute the amount are those that are enacted or substantively enacted by the reporting date.

Current taxes are recognised in profit or loss except to the extent that the tax relates to items recognised outside profit or loss, either in other comprehensive income or directly in equity.

Deferred tax

Deferred tax is provided using the liability method on temporary differences at the reporting date between the tax bases of assets and liabilities and their carrying amounts for financial reporting purposes.

Deferred tax liabilities are recognised for all temporary differences, except:

•          where the deferred tax liability arises from the initial recognition of goodwill or of an asset or liability in a transaction that is not a business combination and, at the time of the transaction, affects neither the accounting profit nor taxable profit or loss; and

•          in respect of taxable temporary differences associated with investments in subsidiaries where the timing of the reversal of the temporary differences can be controlled and it is probable that the temporary differences will not reverse in the foreseeable future.

Deferred tax assets are recognised for all deductible temporary differences, carry forward of unused tax credits and unused tax losses, to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which the deductible temporary differences, and the carry forward of unused tax credits and unused tax losses can be utilised except:

•          where the deferred tax asset relating to the deductible temporary difference arises from the initial recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction that is not a business combination and, at the time of the transaction, affects neither the accounting profit nor taxable profit or loss; and

•          in respect of deductible temporary differences associated with investments in subsidiaries, deferred tax assets are recognised only to the extent that it is probable that the temporary differences will reverse in the foreseeable future and taxable profit will be available against which the temporary differences can be utilised.

The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at each reporting date and reduced to the extent that it is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profit will be available to allow all or part of the deferred tax asset to be utilised.

Unrecognised deferred tax assets are reassessed at each reporting date and are recognised to the extent that it has become probable that future taxable profit will allow the deferred tax assets to be utilised.

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply to the year when the asset is realised or the liability is settled, based on tax rates and tax laws that have been enacted or substantively enacted at the reporting date.

Deferred tax relating to items recognised outside profit or loss is recognised outside profit or loss. Deferred tax items are recognised in correlation to the underlying transaction either in other comprehensive income or directly in equity and deferred tax arising from a business combination is adjusted against goodwill on acquisition.

Deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities are offset, if a legally enforceable right exists to set off current tax assets against current tax liabilities and the deferred taxes relate to the same taxable entity and the same taxation authority.

2.17 Current and Non-Current Classification

The Group present assets and liabilities in the statements of financial position based on current and non-current classification.

An asset is classified as current when it is:

(i)            expected to be realised or intended to be sold or consumed in normal operating cycle;

(ii)           held primarily for the purpose of trading;

(iii)          expected to be realised within 12 months after the reporting period; or

(iv)         cash or cash equivalents unless restricted from being exchanged or used to settle a liability for at least 12 months after the reporting period.

All other assets are classified as non-current.

A liability is classified as current when:

(i)            it is expected to be settled in normal operating cycle;

(ii)           it is held primarily for the purpose of trading;

(iii)          it is due to be settled within 12 months after the reporting period; or

(iv)         there is no unconditional right to defer the settlement of the liability for at least 12 months after the reporting period.

All other liabilities are classified as non-current.

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are classified as non-current assets and liabilities, respectively.

2.18 Borrowing Costs

Borrowing costs that are not directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset are recognised in profit or loss using the effective interest method.

Other operating income comprises income that arises from the company's ordinary activities but is not derived from the principal revenue-generating activities. This includes rental income, hostel services, and gains on disposal of non-current asset held for sale, unrealised exchange difference arising from foreign currency transactions.

3.         SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING JUDGEMENTS AND ESTIMATES

The preparation of the Group's financial statements requires management to make judgements, estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of revenues, expenses, assets and liabilities, and the disclosure of contingent liabilities at the reporting date. However, uncertainty about these assumptions and estimates could result in outcomes that could require a material adjustment to the carrying amount of the asset or liability affected in the future.

Management believes that there are no instances of application of critical judgement in applying the Group's accounting policies which will have a significant effect on the amounts recognised in the financial statements.

Key Sources of Estimation Uncertainty

The key assumptions concerning the future and other sources of estimation uncertainty at the reporting date that have a significant risk of causing a material adjustment to the carrying amounts of assets and liabilities within the next financial year are set out below:

a)            Depreciation of Property, Plant and Equipment

The estimates for the residual values, useful lives and related depreciation charges for the property, plant and equipment are based on commercial and production factors which could change significantly as a result of technical innovations and competitors' actions in response to the market conditions.

The Group anticipates that the residual values of its property, plant and equipment will be insignificant. As a result, residual values are not being taken into consideration for the computation of the depreciable amount.

Changes in the expected level of usage and technological development could impact the economic useful lives and the residual values of these assets, therefore future depreciation charges could be revised.

b)            Income Taxes

Significant judgement is required in determining the capital allowances and deductibility of certain expenses during the estimation of the provision for income taxes. There are many transactions and calculations for which the ultimate tax determination is uncertain during the ordinary course of business. Where the final tax outcome of these matters is different from the amounts that were initially recorded, such differences will impact the income tax and deferred income tax provisions in the period in which such determination is made.

c)            Impairment of Assets

When the recoverable amount of an asset is determined based on the estimate of the value in-use of the cash-generating unit to which the asset is allocated, the management is required to make an estimate of the expected future cash flows from the cash-generating unit and also to apply a suitable discount rate in order to determine the present value of those cash flows.

d)            Allowance for Impairment

The Group makes allowance for impairment based on an assessment of the recoverability of receivables. Allowances are applied to receivables where events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amounts may not be recoverable.

Management specifically analyses historical bad debt, customer concentration, customer creditworthiness, current economic trends and changes in customer payment terms when making a judgement to evaluate the adequacy of the allowance for impairment. Where the expectation is different from the original estimate, such difference will impact the carrying value of receivables.

e)            Fair Value Estimates for Certain Financial Assets and Liabilities

The Group carries certain financial assets and liabilities at fair value, which requires extensive use of accounting estimates and judgement. While significant components of fair value measurement were determined using verifiable objective evidence, the amount of changes in fair value would differ if the Group used different valuation methodologies. Any changes in fair value of these assets and liabilities would affect profit and equity.

f)             Deferred tax assets

Deferred tax assets are recognised for all unused tax losses, unabsorbed capital allowances and other deductible temporary differences to the extent that it is probable that taxable profit will be available against which the unused tax losses, unabsorbed capital allowances and other deductible temporary differences can be utilised. Significant management judgement is required to determine the amount of deferred tax assets that can be recognised, based upon the likely timing and level of future taxable profits.

Basis of accounting

The financial statements have been prepared in accordance with the historical cost convention and in accordance with United Kingdom Accounting Standards, including Financial Reporting Standard 101 Reduced Disclosure Framework (United Kingdom Generally Accepted Accounting Practice), and the Companies Act 2006. The financial statements present information about the Company as an individual entity and the principal accounting policies are described below. They have all been applied consistently throughout the period.

Reduced disclosure exemptions

The Company is a qualifying entity for the purposes of FRS 101 Reduced Disclosure Framework and has taken advantage of the following disclosure exemptions available under that Standard

•          the requirements of IFRS 7 Financial Instruments: Disclosures, as equivalent disclosures are included in the consolidated financial statements of the Group in which the Company is consolidated; and

•          the requirements of IAS 24 Related Party Disclosures to disclose transactions entered into between two or more members of the Group, provided that any subsidiary which is a party to the transaction is wholly owned by a member of the Group.

Going concern

At 30 June 2026 the Company had net current assets of £1,325,756. The Company has assessed its ongoing costs with cash generated by its subsidiaries to ensure that it can continue to settle its debts as they fall due.

The Directors have, after careful consideration of the factors set out above, concluded that it is appropriate to adopt the going concern basis for the preparation of the financial statements and the financial statements do not include any adjustments that would result if the going concern basis was not appropriate.

Investments

Investments held as fixed assets are stated at cost less provision for impairment.

Tax

Current tax, including UK corporation tax and foreign tax, is provided at amounts expected to be paid (or recovered) using the tax rates and laws that have been enacted or substantively enacted by the balance sheet date.

Deferred tax is recognised in respect of all timing differences that have originated but not reversed at the balance sheet date where transactions or events that result in an obligation to pay more tax in the future or a right to pay less tax in the future have occurred at the balance sheet date. Timing differences are differences between the Company's taxable profits and its results as stated in the financial statements that arise from the inclusion of gains and losses in tax assessments in periods different from those in which they are recognised in the financial statements. A net deferred tax asset is regarded as recoverable and therefore recognised only when, on the basis of all available evidence, it can be regarded as more likely than not that there will be suitable taxable profits from which the future reversal of the underlying timing differences can be deducted.

Financial instruments

Financial assets and liabilities are recognised in the statement of financial position when the Company has become a party to the contractual provisions of the instruments.

The Company only enters into basic financial instruments transactions that result in the recognition of financial assets and liabilities like trade and other debtors and creditors and loans to related parties.

Debtors

Short-term debtors are measured at transaction price, less any impairment. Loans and receivables are measured initially at fair value and are measured subsequently at amortised cost using the effective interest method, less any impairment.

Creditors

Short-term trade creditors are measured at the transaction price. Other financial liabilities, including bank loans, are measured initially at fair value and are measured subsequently at amortised cost using the effective interest method.

data.title: DoorDash’s $17B Instacart Deal Draws Significant Street Attention – A Look At What Analysts Have To Say
data.description:
Key points:
  • Cantor Fitzgerald, Bernstein and Morgan Stanley raised their CART price targets to $65, citing limited prospects for a competing bid.
  • Needham lowered its DASH price target to $235 from $265, while Wells Fargo cut its target to $200 from $230; both maintained their existing ratings, with Wells Fargo expressing mixed views on the acquisition, The Fly reported.
  • According to Koyfin data, 34 of 42 analysts rate DASH ‘Buy’ or ‘Strong Buy’, while the remaining eight rate it ‘Hold’. 

DoorDash (DASH) and Instacart (CART) drew investor attention on Friday after multiple analysts revised their ratings and price targets following the companies’ $17 billion acquisition agreement announced Thursday.

Needham lowered its price target on DoorDash to $235 from $265 while maintaining a ‘Buy’ rating, according to The Fly. The firm views the Instacart acquisition positively from strategic and financial standpoints but said regulatory risk remains the biggest question. Needham added that DoorDash is better positioned to integrate the business and capture synergies following its technology replatforming, The Fly reported.

DASH shares traded 1% higher, while CART shares traded 1.5% lower at the time of writing.

According to Koyfin data, 34 out of 42 analysts covering DASH rate the stock ‘Buy’ or ‘Strong Buy’, while eight rate it ‘Hold’. The 12-month price target ranges from $172 to $350, with an average of $256.18.

Meanwhile, 18 out of 30 analysts covering CART rate it ‘Hold’, while 12 rate the stock ‘Buy’ or ‘Strong Buy’, according to Koyfin data. The 12-month price target ranges from $46 to $65, with an average of $58.56.

Analysts Reassess Instacart After $65-Per-Share Deal

According to The Fly, Cantor Fitzgerald downgraded Instacart to ‘Neutral’ from ‘Overweight’ and raised its price target to $65 from $63, citing the pending takeover. Bernstein also lowered its rating to ‘Market Perform’ from ‘Outperform’ and raised its target to $65 from $60. Bernstein expects the deal to pass, The Fly reported.

According to The Fly, Citizens downgraded Instacart’s rating to ‘Market Perform’ from ‘Outperform’ without a price target, saying it does not expect another bidder to outbid DoorDash.

Wedbush views consolidation as valuable for DoorDash and sees Instacart’s technology and tools as additive to the fastest-growing part of DoorDash’s business. According to The Fly, the firm said the deal is not expected to close until late 2027 or early 2028.

data.title: Fed Needs to Implement at Least Two More Rate Increases, Dallas Fed's Logan Says
data.description:
By Jessica Coacci

The Federal Reserve needs to implement at least two more 25-basis-point rate increases given the current economic outlook after the Fed voted to hold interest rates steady this week, according to Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan.

Without any monetary-policy restraint, inflation will continue to trend above target unless unexpected shocks occur, Logan said at an event Friday in Davidson, N.C.

There had been speculation that Logan would dissent at October's FOMC meeting, given her previous calls for tighter monetary policy and a previous dissent she gave in July. On Friday, she offered more explanation to why she instead supported the committee's decision to hold interest rates where they are.

Financial markets have been volatile in response to news on the technology-investment outlook and geopolitical developments, she said. In such an environment, adjusting policy more gradually can help households, businesses and market participants adapt to higher rates and reduce the risk that economic activity deteriorates more sharply than necessary, she added.

Moreover, Logan said the precise timing of each rate increase has little effect on the longer-term rates most borrowers pay as long as market participants understand the Federal Open Market Committee's policy plans.

In addition, skipping a meeting of rate increases doesn't change the monetary-policy destination, Logan argued.

"By making the destination clear, the FOMC can better help the economy adapt and obtain the promised benefits of a skip," she explained.

Given the current outlook, the end goal should be to make policy modestly restrictive to sustainably deliver both maximum employment and stable prices, Logan said

data.title: Week ahead: BoE announcement, non-farm payrolls in focus

On Monday half-year results from Ryanair are due, while in the US, quarterly results from Apple and Palantir will be eyed. On the macro front, the S&P Global UK manufacturing PMI for October will be among the highlights.

AJ Bell analysts Russ Mould, Danni Hewson and Dan Coatsworth said: "It’s trick or treat time for new CEO John Ternus who has an opportunity to put his stamp on Apple’s AI strategy and future direction.

"Apple’s decision to raise the starting prices of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max could ease margin pressure from rising component costs, but investors will be watching for signs of consumer pushback.

"With the shares trading close to all-time highs, Apple’s premium valuation means investors will be looking for more than Apple’s customary earnings beat.

"With only nine days of iPhone 18 Pro sales and no iPhone Duo revenue in the quarter, the market reaction is likely to be driven by Christmas guidance. Management may also be expected to address ‘Crackgate’ with reports on social media of problems with the screens on the new Duo model."

On Tuesday, Primark owner Associated British Foods will release full-year results, while TP Icap, Hiscox and IWG will put out third-quarter trading updates. Across the pond, AMD, Shopify and Pfizer are slated to report Q3 results.

Investors will also look out for the latest policy announcement from the Reserve Bank of Australia.

Wednesday will be busy on the UK corporate front, with trading updates from Barratt Redrow, Coca-Cola HBC, JD Wetherspoon, Lancashire Holdings, Prudential and Smith & Nephew, and half-year results from Trainline.

In the US, quarterly results from Arm, Qualcomm, McDonald’s and Uber Technologies will be in focus.

On the macro front, preliminary eurozone inflation figures for October will be out, along with UK and eurozone PMIs for October.

On Thursday, the corporate calendar will be busy again, with half-year results from Auto Trader, BT Group and Tate & Lyle, Q3 results from Helios Towers and a trading and operations update from Harbour Energy. Trading updates from Next, Vistry Group, Croda, Howden Joinery, Morgan Sindall and OSB Group will also be released.

In the US, quarterly earnings from ConocoPhillips and Cloudflare will be in focus.

In the UK, all eyes will be on the latest policy announcement from the Bank of England, which is widely expected to raise interest rates by 25 basis points to 4%. This would mark the first move in the base rate of 2026.

Rabobank expects the MPC to raise Bank Rate to 4% in a 7-2 split vote. "Whether they like it or not, persistent energy inflation is increasingly forcing the MPC’s hand, even as there is limited evidence of broader second-round effects," it said.

"We have raised our 2027 inflation forecast to 3.9%, driven primarily by higher energy price forecasts.

"We therefore add a second 25bp hike in February 2027, taking Bank Rate to 4.25%, with further moves remaining largely dependent on the situation in the Middle East."

On Friday, British Airways and Iberia owner IAG will release third-quarter earnings. On the macro calendar, the US non-farm payrolls report for October will be in the spotlight, along with average earnings and the unemployment rate.
